title: Chronic diarrhoea in a 21-year-old university student
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 21-year-old university student in general practice with 12 weeks of pale, floating loose stools, fatigue, weight loss and bloating. He mentions an itchy rash on both knees only if asked, and he has a family history of type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease. The candidate then interprets a photograph of the rash, his blood tests and his coeliac serology, recognises coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis and iron and folate deficiency, and plans confirmation, nutritional assessment, family screening and safety netting.
focus: Chronic diarrhoea in a young adult: excluding red flags, finding the rash, and working up coeliac disease
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. John Johnson, a 21-year-old university student, has come to the clinic because he has had diarrhoea. Your supervising GP has asked you to assess him.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Johnson and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you a clinical photograph, Mr Johnson's blood tests and his coeliac serology. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are John Johnson, a 21-year-old arts student. You are polite and a little embarrassed talking about your bowels. The diarrhoea is getting you down. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've had this really bad diarrhoea for a while now, and it's starting to worry me."

The diarrhoea (give only when asked):

  • It has been going on for about 12 weeks.
  • You go 3 to 4 times a day.
  • It is runny and loose.
  • Only if asked specifically about what it looks like: it is light coloured and floats in the toilet. There is no blood, no black or tarry poo and no mucus.
  • Nothing makes it better or worse.
  • It isn't going away, and overall you feel worse.
  • You don't know what is causing it.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • You are tired all the time.
  • You have lost weight. You don't know how much, but your clothes are looser.
  • You have gone off your food.
  • You feel bloated, you have a lot of wind, and you get indigestion.
  • Only if asked specifically about the skin or a rash: for about 4 weeks you have had a rash on both knees. It is red, has little blisters and is very itchy. You have been scratching it.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Tummy pain or cramps (apart from the bloating), or pain that gets better after opening your bowels.
  • Blood in your poo, mouth ulcers, or sore or red eyes.
  • Recent travel, drinking untreated water, anyone around you being sick, fevers or vomiting.
  • Feeling hot or sweaty when others aren't, a racing or pounding heart, or a shake in your hands.
  • Night sweats or lumps anywhere.
  • Joint pain or swelling.
  • Being very thirsty or passing a lot of urine.
  • Stress or low mood before this started. The diarrhoea itself is upsetting you, but you don't feel depressed.

Past medical history: nothing. No operations.

Medications: none. No recent antibiotics and nothing from the chemist.

Allergies: none known.

Family history:

  • Mother: an overactive thyroid (if asked, she was told it was Graves' disease) and type 1 diabetes.
  • Older sister: type 1 diabetes.
  • No one in the family has had bowel problems or bowel cancer that you know of.

Social history:

  • You don't smoke. You drink socially and don't binge. No drugs.
  • You study arts at university and live in university accommodation.
  • You run twice a week.
  • You eat balanced, home-cooked meals. Only if asked about bread, pasta or cereal: you eat them most days, and you haven't cut anything out of your diet.
  • You have good friends and family and feel well supported.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I've got no idea what's causing it."
  • Concerns: it is affecting your studies and your social life. You have stopped going out because you need to be near a toilet, and you find it distressing.
  • Expectation: "I just want to know what's going on."

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Do you think it's something serious?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: thin young man who looks tired. Alert and comfortable. Weight 64 kg, height 180 cm, BMI 19.8. The practice record shows 68 kg eight months ago.
  • Observations: HR 78 regular, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C. Capillary BGL (if asked) 5.4 mmol/L, random.
  • Hands: no clubbing, no koilonychia. Palmar creases slightly pale. No tremor.
  • Face and mouth: mild conjunctival pallor. Angular cheilitis at both corners of the mouth. No mouth ulcers. No jaundice.
  • Eyes and neck: no exophthalmos or lid lag. No goitre or thyroid nodules. No cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen: mildly distended, no scars. Soft and non-tender, with no masses and no hepatosplenomegaly. Tympanic to percussion. Bowel sounds active.
  • Skin of the knees: there is a rash on the front of both knees, with scratch marks. Say: "A photograph of the rash will be shown to you in Part 2."
  • Elbows, buttocks and scalp (if examined): no rash.
  • Joints: no swelling or tenderness.
  • Perianal inspection and rectal examination (if offered, with a chaperone): perianal skin normal, no skin tags or fistulae. Soft pale stool on the glove, no blood.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms John's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language, is sensitive to his embarrassment, and acknowledges how distressing the diarrhoea is and its effect on his study and social life.
History
Characterises the diarrhoea:

kids.x: Duration, frequency and course: 12 weeks, 3 to 4 times a day, loose and runny, nothing makes it better or worse, getting worse overall.
Asks what the stool looks like: pale and floating (suggesting fat malabsorption), with no blood, melaena or mucus.

check.x: Asks about associated and constitutional symptoms: fatigue, weight loss (amount unknown), loss of appetite, bloating, flatulence and indigestion.
Asks specifically about a skin rash and characterises it: both knees, about 4 weeks, red, blistering and very itchy.
check.d: John mentions the rash only if asked about the skin or a rash.

check.x: Takes a targeted review that screens for red flags and common differentials:
check.d: Award the parent item for at least 5 of the 6 groups.

kids.x: Inflammatory bowel disease: blood in the stool, abdominal pain, mouth ulcers, eye or joint symptoms.
Infection: travel, untreated water, sick contacts, fever and vomiting.
Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, palpitations and tremor.
Malignancy: night sweats and lumps, alongside the weight loss.
Irritable bowel syndrome: pain linked to and relieved by defecation, and psychological stressors.

check.x: Asks about his diet, including whether he eats gluten-containing foods (bread, pasta, cereal most days) and whether he has cut anything out (he has not).
Takes the past medical history, medications (including recent antibiotics and over-the-counter medicines) and allergies: nil, nil, none known.
Asks about family history of autoimmune, thyroid and bowel disease: mother has hyperthyroidism and type 1 diabetes, older sister has type 1 diabetes, no known bowel disease.
Takes a social history: non-smoker, drinks socially without binges, no drugs, arts student in university accommodation, runs twice a week, eats balanced home-cooked meals, well supported.
check.d: Award for smoking, alcohol, occupation or living situation, and support.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: no idea of the cause, distressed by the impact on study and socialising, wants to know what is going on, and responds honestly to his question about whether it is serious, without false reassurance (tests are needed; the likely causes are treatable).
Examination
Asks for vital signs, weight and BMI, and compares the weight with the practice record (about 4 kg lost in 8 months).
Looks for signs of anaemia and malnutrition: conjunctival and palmar pallor, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, and also clubbing.
Looks for signs of hyperthyroidism: tremor, pulse, goitre and eye signs.
Examines the abdomen: inspection, palpation for tenderness, masses and hepatosplenomegaly, percussion and bowel sounds (mildly distended, soft, non-tender).
Inspects the skin of both knees and the other extensor sites (elbows, buttocks, scalp) for the rash.
check.d: Award for inspecting both knees plus naming or offering at least one other extensor site (elbows, buttocks or scalp).

check.x: Checks the mouth for ulcers and the neck for lymph nodes, and offers a perianal inspection and rectal examination with a chaperone.
Interpretation
Interprets the clinical photograph:

kids.x: Describes it: symmetrical clusters of small red papules and vesicles with erosions, excoriations and crusts on the extensor surfaces of both knees.
Names it as dermatitis herpetiformis, the skin manifestation of coeliac disease.

check.x: Interprets the full blood count and haematinics: microcytic anaemia (Hb 116, MCV 74) with low ferritin and transferrin saturation from iron deficiency, low folate and normal B12, fitting malabsorption from the proximal small bowel.

Interprets the other bloods: normal TSH and free T4 (against hyperthyroidism), normal CRP (does not support IBD, though does not exclude it), and a mildly raised ALT, which can occur in coeliac disease and is rechecked on treatment.

Interprets the coeliac serology: tTG-IgA more than 10 times the upper limit with positive EMA and DGP, and a normal total IgA so there is no IgA deficiency to cause a false negative; valid because he is eating gluten.

Gives coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis as the most likely diagnosis, and at least three differentials each with a feature for or against (for example Crohn's disease, hyperthyroidism, giardiasis, irritable bowel syndrome).
Management
Tells him to keep eating gluten as normal until the biopsy is done, because stopping it can make the biopsy falsely normal.
Refers to gastroenterology for gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to confirm the diagnosis.
Arranges a skin biopsy of the rash (lesional for histology and perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence), or refers to dermatology, and notes dapsone for itch is a specialist option.
Completes the nutritional and associated-condition work-up: vitamin D and calcium, and fasting glucose or HbA1c.
check.d: Award for vitamin D, calcium and a glucose test. Bone density testing is acceptable as an extra.

check.x: Replaces iron and folate (oral iron; folic acid, safe because B12 is normal), with IV iron if oral iron fails or is not tolerated.
check.d: Award for oral iron plus folic acid. Doses not required.

check.x: Plans a lifelong strict gluten-free diet once the diagnosis is confirmed (no wheat, rye, barley or oats), with referral to a dietitian and Coeliac Australia.
check.d: Award for a lifelong strict gluten-free diet started after confirmation, plus dietitian referral. Naming the grains is desirable but not required.

check.x: Advises that his first-degree relatives (mother and sister) are offered coeliac serology.
Safety netting

Explains to John in plain words that the results strongly suggest coeliac disease, a reaction to gluten that damages the lining of the small bowel, and that it explains the diarrhoea, tiredness, weight loss, low iron and the rash.
check.d: Marked from the final question, when John is back in the room.

check.x: Tells him to see the GP the same day or go to the ED for blood or black stools, fever, severe tummy pain, persistent vomiting, signs of dehydration (dizziness, very little urine), feeling faint or breathless, or rapid further weight loss.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words linked to where to go. A rash that spreads or looks infected, and marked thirst with passing a lot of urine, also count as red flags.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review after the gastroscopy and biopsy results, with repeat blood tests to check that the iron and folate are improving.

part2.lead: At John's first visit your supervisor photographed the rash on his knees and ordered blood tests. John has come back a week later for the results. Here are the photograph and his results.
part2.patient:
During the final question only, ask once each:

  • "Can I just cut out gluten now and see if I feel better?"
  • "Is this why I've been so tired?"

You are relieved to have an explanation. If the candidate uses jargon such as "serology", "duodenal biopsy" or "malabsorption" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Clinical photograph of both knees
handover.result:
Clinical photograph: both knees, anterior view, taken by the supervising GP at the first visit.

Clinical details: 21-year-old man with 12 weeks of loose pale stools; very itchy rash on both knees for 4 weeks.

Distribution and morphology to be described by the candidate.
handover.model:
• Findings (examiner only): distribution symmetrical, on the extensor surfaces of both knees. Lesions: grouped clusters of small (2 to 4 mm) erythematous papules and a few small, grouped vesicles, some intact. Secondary changes: many lesions scratched open, with erosions, excoriations and small haemorrhagic crusts. No scale or plaques, no pustules, no honey-coloured crusting; the surrounding skin is normal.
  • Read: symmetrical clusters of small erythematous papules and vesicles, with erosions, excoriations and crusts, on the extensor surfaces of both knees.
  • For John: this is dermatitis herpetiformis, the itchy blistering skin manifestation of coeliac disease. It fits his 4 weeks of a very itchy, blistering rash on both knees. The symmetry and extensor site argue against herpes simplex, impetigo and contact dermatitis. Scabies and eczema are less likely given the distribution and the vesicles.
  • What it changes: it points strongly to coeliac disease. A skin biopsy confirms it: lesional skin for histology and perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence, which shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae. The rash settles with a gluten-free diet over months; dapsone relieves the itch quickly and is started by a specialist.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Collected at the first visit. Blood film: hypochromic microcytic red cells with pencil cells, consistent with iron deficiency.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 116 with MCV 74, low MCH and high RDW: a microcytic anaemia. Ferritin 6, low iron and transferrin saturation, high transferrin: iron deficiency. Folate low, B12 normal. Platelets mildly raised, as often seen in iron deficiency. ALT mildly raised at 46 with otherwise normal LFTs; albumin low-normal. CRP, TSH and free T4 normal. Renal function and electrolytes normal.
  • For John: iron and folate are absorbed in the proximal small bowel (duodenum and jejunum), which coeliac disease damages; B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum and is spared. A young man with no blood loss and a balanced diet should not be iron deficient, so malabsorption is the explanation. A normal TSH and free T4 exclude hyperthyroidism. A normal CRP does not support IBD but does not exclude it. A mild ALT rise is common in untreated coeliac disease.
  • What it changes: replace iron and folate (B12 is normal, so folic acid is safe). Add vitamin D, calcium and a fasting glucose or HbA1c. Recheck the ALT on the gluten-free diet and investigate it if it does not settle.

handover.label: Coeliac serology
handover.result: Collected at the first visit. Clinical notes on the request: chronic diarrhoea, itchy rash on both knees; patient eating a normal gluten-containing diet.
handover.model:
• Read: tTG-IgA 210 U/mL, more than 10 times the upper limit. EMA-IgA positive at a titre of 1:320. DGP-IgG raised. Total IgA normal.
  • For John: strongly positive, concordant serology makes coeliac disease very likely. Total IgA is normal, so there is no IgA deficiency to cause a falsely negative IgA-based test. He has been eating gluten normally, so the result is valid.
  • What it changes: in Australia, adults still need a gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to confirm the diagnosis, so refer to gastroenterology and tell him to keep eating gluten until the biopsy. Do not start the gluten-free diet yet. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is not needed to make the diagnosis here, but helps if the biopsy is equivocal (a negative result virtually excludes coeliac disease).

rows.n: more than 10 times the upper limit

ask: You are now discussing John with your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of John Johnson, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of John now, here in general practice.
John is back in the room. Explain to him what the results mean, what happens next and when he should seek help.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; John Johnson, 21, arts student.
  • Situation: results strongly suggest coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis.
  • Background: 12 weeks of pale, floating loose stools 3 to 4 times a day; fatigue, weight loss (68 to 64 kg), bloating; itchy blistering rash on both knees for 4 weeks. No blood or pain. Mother has hyperthyroidism and T1DM, sister T1DM. Eating gluten.
  • Assessment: photo: symmetrical grouped papules and vesicles with erosions on extensor knees, dermatitis herpetiformis. Microcytic anaemia with iron and folate deficiency, normal B12. TSH and CRP normal, ALT mildly raised. tTG-IgA over 10 times normal, EMA and DGP positive, total IgA normal.
  • Recommendation: gastroenterology referral for duodenal biopsy while still eating gluten, skin biopsy, iron and folate, further bloods, dietitian after confirmation.

Most likely: coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis, causing iron and folate deficiency. Supporting: pale floating stools (fat malabsorption), weight loss, fatigue, bloating, the rash, family autoimmune disease, proximal small bowel malabsorption, strongly positive serology with normal IgA.

  • Crohn's disease: for: young, weight loss, iron deficiency. Against: no blood, pain or mouth ulcers, normal CRP.
  • Hyperthyroidism: for: diarrhoea, weight loss, mother affected. Against: no symptoms, normal TSH and free T4.
  • Giardiasis: for: floating stools, bloating, flatulence. Against: no travel, untreated water or contacts.
  • Irritable bowel syndrome: for: bloating, distress. Against: weight loss, steatorrhoea and anaemia are red flags.

1. Keep eating gluten until the biopsy; do not start the diet yet.
  2. Refer to gastroenterology for gastroscopy and duodenal biopsies.
  3. Skin biopsy (lesional and perilesional for direct immunofluorescence) or dermatology referral; dapsone for itch is a specialist option.
  4. Further tests: vitamin D, calcium, fasting glucose or HbA1c (bone density scan can be arranged once the diagnosis is confirmed).
  5. Replace iron (about 100 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days) and folic acid 5 mg orally daily (about 4 months); IV iron if oral fails.
  6. After confirmation: lifelong strict gluten-free diet (no wheat, rye, barley or oats), dietitian and Coeliac Australia.
  7. Family: offer coeliac serology to his mother and sister.

• Explain in plain words: the tests strongly suggest coeliac disease, a reaction to gluten that damages the lining of the small bowel; it explains the diarrhoea, weight loss, rash and low iron (the cause of his tiredness).
  • Cutting out gluten now (his question): not yet; keep eating gluten until the biopsy, then start the gluten-free diet.
  • See the GP the same day or go to the ED for blood or black stools, fever, severe tummy pain, persistent vomiting, dehydration (dizzy, passing little urine), feeling faint or breathless, or rapid weight loss.
  • (optional) rash infected or spreading, very thirsty or passing a lot of urine.
  • Follow-up: GP review after the biopsy; repeat bloods to check iron and folate.

ddx.for: Twelve weeks of pale floating loose stools with weight loss, fatigue and bloating, an itchy blistering rash on both knees, family type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, iron and folate deficiency, and strongly positive tTG-IgA and EMA with normal total IgA.

ddx.dx: Crohn's disease of the small bowel
ddx.for: A young adult with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, fatigue and iron deficiency.
ddx.against: No blood, abdominal pain, mouth ulcers or perianal disease, a normal CRP, and serology and a rash that point to coeliac disease.

ddx.for: Diarrhoea and weight loss with a mother who has hyperthyroidism.
ddx.against: No heat intolerance, palpitations or tremor, no goitre, and a normal TSH and free T4.

ddx.for: Pale floating stools with bloating, flatulence and indigestion.
ddx.against: No travel, untreated water, sick contacts or fever.

ddx.for: A young student with bloating, flatulence and distressing diarrhoea.
ddx.against: Weight loss, pale floating stools and iron deficiency anaemia are red flags that IBS does not explain, and he has no pain linked to defecation.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. John mentions the rash only if asked about his skin or a rash. If the candidate examines the knees, say there is a rash and that a photograph will be shown in Part 2. The description and diagnosis of the rash are marked in Part 2, not Part 1. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the results will come in Part 2. In Part 2 hand over the photograph and both sets of results, then ask the four questions in order. John asks his two questions during the final question.

A high-performing candidate characterises the diarrhoea and asks what the stool looks like, picks up the constitutional symptoms, and asks about a rash. They screen systematically for IBD, infection, hyperthyroidism, malignancy, IBS and diabetes, ask whether he eats gluten, and find the family history of autoimmune disease. They examine for pallor, thyroid signs, the abdomen and the skin. In Part 2 they describe the rash before naming dermatitis herpetiformis, link the iron and folate deficiency to proximal small bowel malabsorption, check the total IgA, tell John to keep eating gluten until the duodenal biopsy, and plan nutritional replacement, a dietitian and family screening.

A borderline candidate takes a generic diarrhoea history without asking about the stool or the skin, labels it IBS or gastroenteritis, misses the significance of the family history, or tells John to start a gluten-free diet straight away.
explain:
Diagnosis

John has coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis, complicated by iron and folate deficiency. He has 12 weeks of loose, pale, floating stools (suggesting fat malabsorption), with fatigue, weight loss, loss of appetite, bloating, flatulence and indigestion. He also has an itchy, blistering rash on both knees, and his mother and sister have autoimmune disease (type 1 diabetes and hyperthyroidism). The photograph, the pattern of nutrient deficiency and the strongly positive serology all point to the same diagnosis.

Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease affects at least 1% of people. It is an immune-mediated inflammation of the small bowel triggered by gluten (in wheat, rye, barley and oats) in genetically susceptible people. Presentations vary widely: classic malabsorption, isolated iron deficiency, fatigue, abdominal symptoms, abnormal liver tests, or no symptoms. Think of it in anyone with chronic diarrhoea and fatigue, especially with a personal or family history of autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes. About 15 to 25% of people with coeliac disease have dermatitis herpetiformis, so asking about a rash is what distinguishes a strong candidate.

Dermatitis herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely itchy rash of grouped papules and vesicles, symmetrically on the extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks and scalp). The vesicles are often scratched away, so erosions, excoriations and crusts may be all that is seen. A skin biopsy confirms it: lesional skin for histology, and perilesional (normal-looking) skin for direct immunofluorescence, which shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae. The rash responds to a gluten-free diet, though this can take months; dapsone gives quick relief of the itch and is started and monitored by a specialist.

Differentials that matter

  • Crohn's disease: small bowel Crohn's can cause malabsorption and iron deficiency. John has no blood, pain, mouth ulcers or perianal disease, and his CRP is normal.
  • Hyperthyroidism: causes diarrhoea and weight loss, and his mother has it, but he has no symptoms or signs and his thyroid function is normal.
  • Giardiasis: causes pale, floating stools, bloating and flatulence, but he has no travel, untreated water or contacts. A stool test for parasites is reasonable if the diagnosis is still in doubt.
  • Irritable bowel syndrome: weight loss, steatorrhoea and anaemia are red flags that must be explained before IBS is considered.
  • Malignancy: screen for night sweats, lumps and weight loss in any chronic diarrhoea history.

Interpreting the results

  • Photograph: symmetrical clusters of papules and vesicles with erosions and crusts on both knees: dermatitis herpetiformis.
  • Blood count and haematinics: a microcytic anaemia with iron deficiency and low folate but normal B12. Iron and folate are absorbed in the proximal small bowel, which coeliac disease affects first; B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Iron deficiency is common in coeliac disease.
  • Other bloods: normal thyroid function and CRP. A mild ALT rise is common in untreated coeliac disease and usually settles on the diet.
  • Serology: tTG-IgA is the first-line test, with total IgA, because IgA deficiency is more common in coeliac disease and causes false-negative IgA-based tests (IgG-based tests such as DGP-IgG are then used). EMA and DGP add support. Serology is only valid while the person is eating gluten. Someone who has already cut out gluten needs a gluten challenge, eating gluten daily for several weeks as Coeliac Australia advises, before testing.

Confirming the diagnosis

In Australian adults, positive serology is confirmed by gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, taken while the person is still eating gluten. In a patient with dermatitis herpetiformis, a skin biopsy showing granular IgA in the dermal papillae confirms coeliac disease; gastroscopy is still usually performed in Australia to assess the mucosa and provide a baseline, and both biopsies require him to keep eating gluten. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain or the person is already gluten free: a negative result virtually excludes coeliac disease, but a positive one is common in the general population and does not confirm it.

Management

  • Do not start the gluten-free diet until the biopsy is done.
  • Assess nutrition and associated conditions: full blood count, iron studies, B12, folate, vitamin D and calcium (bone health) and a bone density (DXA) scan at or soon after diagnosis in adults, thyroid function, and a glucose test given the family history of type 1 diabetes.
  • Replace deficiencies: oral iron (eTG: about 100 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days), with IV iron if oral iron fails or is not tolerated (absorption may be poor until the mucosa heals); folic acid 5 mg orally daily (about 4 months) once B12 is known to be normal.
  • Treatment: a lifelong strict gluten-free diet, avoiding wheat, rye, barley and oats, with dietitian support and Coeliac Australia for education and resources.
  • Family: first-degree relatives have about a 1 in 10 risk and should be offered serology. His mother and sister, who have type 1 diabetes, are at particular risk.

Safety netting and follow-up

He should seek same-day care for blood or black stools, fever, severe pain, vomiting, dehydration or rapid weight loss, and see the GP if the rash becomes infected or he develops thirst and polyuria. Review him after the biopsy, recheck his blood count and iron after a few months of replacement, and repeat the coeliac serology after about 6 to 12 months on the diet to check adherence and response, with ongoing review.

Source: adapted from AMSA MedEd OSCE course, Gastrointestinal, "Diarrhoea History 1".
points: In chronic diarrhoea, ask what the stool looks like: pale, floating stools suggest fat malabsorption, and weight loss, steatorrhoea or anaemia are red flags that rule out a label of IBS until they are explained.

Always ask about a rash: 15 to 25% of people with coeliac disease have dermatitis herpetiformis, an intensely itchy, symmetrical rash of grouped papules and vesicles on the elbows, knees, buttocks and scalp.
Think of coeliac disease in chronic diarrhoea or fatigue with a personal or family history of autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes, and in unexplained iron deficiency.
Test with tTG-IgA and total IgA (IgA deficiency gives false negatives) while the patient is eating gluten; in Australian adults, confirm with duodenal biopsy before starting the diet.
Iron and folate are absorbed in the proximal small bowel, so iron and folate deficiency with a normal B12 fits coeliac disease.
Treatment is a lifelong strict gluten-free diet with dietitian support, plus replacement of deficiencies and serology for first-degree relatives.

imaging.finding: Symmetrical grouped small erythematous papules and vesicles with erosions, excoriations and crusts on the extensor surfaces of both knees
imaging.caption: Clinical photograph of both knees, taken at the first visit.
imaging.alt: Both knees showing symmetrical clusters of small red bumps and blisters with scratch marks and crusts.
